headline: Yesterday’s repetition becomes
today’s skill.
hero.lede: We turned recurring software work across eight coding agents into {count} workflows you can verify. Reuse the same instructions with prompt caching, and let scripts handle predictable steps so the LLM can focus on judgment.
hero.proof: {count} ready-to-use workflows · {categories} categories · 8 supported agents · MIT

benefits.label: Why skills
title: Repeat the work,
not the explanation.
benefits.description: Skills reuse stable instructions and hand predictable procedures to scripts, so the model can focus on decisions that need context.

items.label: Reusable instructions
items.title: Stop rebuilding the same instructions.
items.description: Write the sequence, examples, and safety rules once in SKILL.md. Repeated requests can reuse the same prefix, making prompt caching easier to use on models that support it.

items.label: Deterministic scripts
items.title: Let scripts handle predictable work.
items.description: Use scripts for steps with clear outcomes, such as file discovery, format checks, and data synchronization. The model no longer has to work through the same procedure every time.

items.label: Focused judgment
items.title: Keep the LLM focused on judgment.
items.description: Use the model for requirements, code review, and risk decisions that need context. Record the execution order and completion criteria in the skill.

tagline.label: Repeatable by design
lines: A good prompt disappears after one use.
Turn it into a skill, and it becomes part of how you work.

faq.label: FAQ
faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.description: What to know before you install.

items.question: What exactly is a skill?
items.answer: A skill is a SKILL.md document that defines how an agent should perform a specific task. It includes the execution sequence, safety rules, and output format so repeated requests follow the same standard.

items.question: How is it different from a regular prompt?
items.answer: A prompt disappears when the conversation ends, but a skill remains as a file. You can version it, share it with a team, and call it again by name, such as $review-me.

items.question: Do skills always reduce token usage?
items.answer: No—savings are not guaranteed. Prompt caching depends on the model, instruction length, and whether the same prefix is preserved. Skills are designed to reuse stable instructions and separate scripted steps, which can reduce unnecessary LLM work.

items.question: Which tasks should scripts handle?
items.answer: Tasks whose inputs and outputs can be checked by rules. Scripts handle file discovery, format validation, catalog synchronization, and test execution; the LLM handles interpretation and review.

items.question: Which agents can use these skills?
items.answer: These skills support Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity CLI, Grok Build, Pi, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, and OpenCode. Codex calls the same SKILL.md with $name, while Claude Code uses /name.

items.question: What gets added to my computer?
items.answer: Most agents read the shared copy in ~/.agents/skills. The installer adds links for Claude Code, Antigravity CLI, and Grok Build.

items.question: Can a skill commit or push on its own?
items.answer: Each skill states its safety rules explicitly. For example, git-commit stages only the files it names and makes only ordinary pushes. A force push is possible only in rewrite, which changes history, and only after you explicitly agree. If a push is rejected, it stops and reports what happened.

items.question: Can I install only selected skills?
items.answer: Yes. Replace --skill '*' in the install command with the name of the skill you want. Each skill README also includes its individual install command.

items.question: How do I update installed skills?
items.answer: Run npx skills update chann/skills to update installed skills to the latest version.

items.question: Are there fees or license restrictions?
items.answer: No. The entire repository is open source under the MIT License. You can fork it and adapt the skills to your team’s rules.

chann.summary: Give it one task and it restates the goal in a sentence, picks one of 14 playbooks, and routes each step to the skill that owns it.
chann.whenToUse: When you want a whole task handled, such as a bug fix, a feature, or an investigation, without choosing the skills yourself. Runs only when you type it
chann.result: The goal and the smallest change, the playbook chosen, the skill used at each step, the principles applied, and a final report with labelled evidence

how.summary: Reads the code and explains how a part of the codebase works and where new code belongs.
how.whenToUse: When you need to understand an unfamiliar subsystem or know which module owns something
how.result: An overview, key concepts, runtime flow, a file:line map, and gotchas. Every claim is cited, and anything unread is marked inferred

why.summary: Finds why code is built this way in git history, blame, pull-request and issue discussion, and design notes.
why.whenToUse: When you need a reason the code itself cannot show, such as why a flag is still off or why one approach was chosen
why.result: A decision timeline that quotes the authors, inferences marked, and what the record does not answer

research-brief.summary: Answer a technical question from primary sources, with every claim tiered and version-pinned.
research-brief.whenToUse: When behavior or a specification must be confirmed against official sources you can check again later
research-brief.result: A bottom-line answer with confidence, a tiered claim table, a contradiction ledger, and open questions

recall.summary: Builds a date-ranged report from local agent history (Claude Code, Codex, opencode, agy), or a short brief on where one topic stands now.
recall.whenToUse: When you want a summary of what you did this week, or need to know where you left off before resuming earlier work
recall.result: A Markdown report, or a short brief whose branch, PR, and file claims are checked against live git

catchup.summary: Tells you what changed in this conversation while you were away and which decisions are waiting on you.
catchup.whenToUse: When you come back to an agent that kept working and need to catch up fast
catchup.result: What waits on you first, then what happened, then each decision you must make. Live branch, PR, CI, and agent state are checked first, read-only

diff-summary.summary: Explains a change's purpose, behavior, structure, and test impact with evidence. --md gives Markdown only, and --quiz adds a comprehension quiz.
diff-summary.whenToUse: When you need to understand fast why a range such as main..dev, a branch, a commit, or a PR changed
diff-summary.result: Korean and English Markdown plus an interactive HTML summary. --md skips the HTML, and --quiz adds a quiz with answers

plan-summary.summary: Summarizes the plans, PRDs, specs, and design documents you name as aligned Korean and English reports. --md and --quiz also work.
plan-summary.whenToUse: When a team needs to grasp a document's goals, scope, decisions, dependencies, risks, and open questions quickly
plan-summary.result: Korean and English PS-* Markdown cards plus a self-contained bilingual HTML report. --md gives Markdown only, and --quiz adds matching QZ-* questions

diff-viewer.summary: Render the current Git diff as a readable standalone HTML page.
diff-viewer.whenToUse: When you want to inspect the raw patch in a browser without analysis
diff-viewer.result: A unified or split-view HTML diff

review-me.summary: Review every important choice in a plan or design so nothing is left unresolved.
review-me.whenToUse: Before implementation, when ambiguous choices, boundaries, and failure or recovery conditions must be resolved
review-me.result: Resolved choices, completion criteria for each one, acceptance examples, and an explicit deferral list

arena.summary: Runs one prompt on several candidates, has a judge from another vendor score them against a hidden rubric, and grafts the best parts of the others into the winner by hand.
arena.whenToUse: When you want competing designs or drafts and only the best one kept. Not for mechanical tasks whose shape is already settled
arena.result: The finished artifact, the base chosen and why, the judge's verdict, each graft with its source, what was rejected and why, and the verification result

bug-hunt.summary: Reproduce first, falsify hypotheses in a ledger, and pin the fix with a check that failed first.
bug-hunt.whenToUse: When a bug's cause is not obvious, a test fails intermittently, or something suddenly got slower
bug-hunt.result: A recorded reproduction, a falsification ledger, a failing-first check, and a record under .bug-hunts/

gen-docs.summary: Create or update core project docs while preserving existing wording.
gen-docs.whenToUse: When README, architecture, or usage docs have drifted from the code

unslop.summary: Rewrites AI-written Korean or English so it reads like a person wrote it, without changing the meaning.
unslop.whenToUse: When text sounds machine-made: translation-ese, literal jargon, filler openers, or inflated vocabulary
unslop.result: The rewritten text and a short note on what kind of change was made. Text that is already fine is barely touched

build-reinstall.summary: Build the current project, reinstall it with project-owned commands, and verify that the installed result matches the new build.
build-reinstall.whenToUse: After code work is complete and a local app or CLI must be replaced with the new build
build-reinstall.result: Build, reinstall, smoke-check, and SHA-256 installed-artifact evidence

interrogate.summary: Tries to break a code change and reports defects tagged with severity and proof level. It never applies fixes.
interrogate.whenToUse: When you review a PR, commit, branch, or working tree before merging
interrogate.result: A Markdown review and a bilingual HTML review, each finding carrying its proof level (cited, traced, ran, reproduced) and the proof. --md gives Markdown only

blast-radius.summary: Finds what a change could break outside its diff and proves the fact it is safe because of, running real code in a temporary directory.
blast-radius.whenToUse: When even a small change makes you worry about its reach before you merge
blast-radius.result: The safety fact with its proof level, risks with file:line, what was checked and cleared, and the cheapest check to run before merging

git-commit.summary: Splits changes into Conventional Commits. Arguments pick the mode: push, realtime, deploy, or rewrite.
git-commit.whenToUse: When you want mixed changes turned into reviewable commits, or verified checkpoints committed, pushed, or deployed as you work. Also reachable as gcr, gcpr, and gcpd
git-commit.result: Commits staged by explicit path, ordinary pushes, and deploys only through documented repository settings. rewrite redoes commit messages

git-merge.summary: Merges the current branch into main, dev, or a local branch you name, and deletes the merged source branch unless it is protected.
git-merge.whenToUse: When you fold a feature branch into main or dev. With no argument it merges into the repository default branch
git-merge.result: A confirmed plan, a merge that is not pushed, and a source branch deleted only with git branch -d

git-resolve-conflicts.summary: Finish a stopped merge or rebase while keeping both intents, and record what was dropped.
git-resolve-conflicts.whenToUse: When a merge, rebase, or cherry-pick has stopped on conflicts and must be completed rather than aborted
git-resolve-conflicts.result: A classified conflict inventory, a resolution ledger, the project's check results, and a completed operation

git-cleanup.summary: Removes local branches that are already merged and worktrees that are finished, after you confirm one plan.
git-cleanup.whenToUse: When merged branches and finished worktrees have piled up and you want them cleared safely
git-cleanup.result: Each worktree removed and branch deleted with the proof it was merged, plus what was kept and why. --force and -D are never used

swarm.summary: Fans work out to subagents or hands it to another coding agent or model, then returns one report.
swarm.whenToUse: When you want parallel work through subagents, a second opinion from another model, or the load spread across quota. To race candidates for one winner, use arena
swarm.result: The done-predicate verdict, a table of each worker's PASS, ISSUES, or BLOCKED result, why each route was chosen, and a call tree

long-task.summary: Run a large project end to end through milestones and verification cycles.
long-task.whenToUse: When delegating an autonomous implementation that will take several hours
long-task.result: An execution record covering planning, parallel work, review, and completion checks

handoff.summary: Writes an evidence-based handoff document for frontend, backend, or the next session. Pick frontend, backend, or session.
handoff.whenToUse: When API changes go to client developers, server changes go to backend developers, or this session must be picked up by a fresh agent
handoff.result: A document under .handoffs/ that separates what is proven from what is not and ends with a prompt to continue from

skill-forge.summary: Author a skill package against the contract and publish every surface it needs.
skill-forge.whenToUse: When adding, renaming, or repairing a skill so it follows the same rules as the rest
skill-forge.result: SKILL.md, Codex descriptor, slash command, evals, catalog, four locales, counts, and tests

skill-audit.summary: Check every packaged skill against the nine contract rules and report what fails.
skill-audit.whenToUse: Before a merge or release, to confirm packages and the catalog have not drifted apart
skill-audit.result: A violation list naming rule, skill, and file, plus a non-zero exit code

reflect.summary: Keeps only the lessons from a session or repository history that will still hold later, and puts each where it is enforced most strongly.
reflect.whenToUse: When you want what this work taught turned into a rule so the same mistake is not repeated. Choose session (the default) or repo
reflect.result: Three lists to approve before any edit: Accepted, Rejected, and Backlog. After approval, each edit is proven by a check that fails on the past mistake first
